messages.body_plain:
On Jul 27, 2012, at 7:05 PM, Elisa Zhang wrote:

> My question is what parameters you think we should use for scanone(). I've tried setting the phenotype distribution to normal and binary (with >280days as the cutoff). This results in a rather lopsided binary curve though. I've also played around with not binary-izing the genotypes. However, none of these settings give me significant loci. I know it's quite possible that our data just does not contain significant loci, but I wanted to ask for any advice you have before throwing in the towel.

You could try different binary splits, but I don't think it's likely to provide additional information over just doing Haley-Knott regression (method="hk").  You could also try the rank-based approach (model="np").  The different methods with model="normal" ("hk", "em", "imp", ...) shouldn't make much difference since you have dense marker genotypes.

> Another question is, how valid would it be to use a t.test() in R to evaluate my phenotype values vs. my two genotype groups, in place of the marker regression method in scanone() ? (No assumptions of phenotype distribution go into this.) Someone else in my group did this and got lower p-values than what scanone() returns.

Doing a t-test at each marker should be essentially the same as scanone.  If you plot -log(p-value) from the t-test against the LOD scores from scanone, I expect you'll see a nearly monotonic relationship.  The main difference would be in the handling of missing of genotype data; scanone makes use of surrounding markers to impute genotypes, while with a t-test at a marker, you'd have to just omit individuals with missing genotypes.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] output summary.fitqtl in a text file
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] output summary.fitqtl in a text file
messages.body_plain:
The output of fitqtl contains several components; you'll want to pull out just one of them to write to a file.  Probably, you want the results of the "drop-one-qtl" analysis. Here's an example:

  data(hyper)
  hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=2.5)
  qtl <- makeqtl(hyper, chr=c(1,4,6,15), pos=c(50, 50, 50, 50), what="prob")
  qtl <- refineqtl(hyper, qtl=qtl, method="hk", formula = y~q1+q2+q3*q4)
  out.fq <- fitqtl(hyper, qtl=qtl, formula= y~q1+q2+q3*q4, method="hk")
  droponetab <- summary(out.fq)$result.drop
  write.table(droponetab, file="droponetab.txt", sep="\t", quote=FALSE, row.names=TRUE)

karl

messages.subject: Re: mqmscan singular matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hey Angovy,

The singular matrix can have multiple causes:

(1) Most often: Map problems, this is caused by either
  1 Markers at the same position (with different genotypes) or
  2 A map on which there are markers which behave as unlinked (so the chromosome has map expansion, and the total length is too long)

This can be checked by using:

plot.map(pull.map(cross),est.map(cross))

If a or multiple chromosome(s) from the map expands significantly then this is a good indication that this is happening

To debug this problem and find the offending chromosome, just scan the chromosomes 1 by 1, and record the chromosomes that cannot be scanned.
(I use the pheno2geno package (not yet on CRAN) developed by a student of mine to drop chromosomes by name (function removeChromosomes from
https://github.com/KonradZych/phenotypes2genotypes )

in Arabidopsis (which has 5 chromosomes)

new_cross <- removeChromosomes(cross,c('2','3','4','5'))
res_c1 <- mqmscan(new_cross)

new_cross <- removeChromosomes(cross,c('1','3','4','5'))
res_c2 <- mqmscan(new_cross)

Then once you identified the chromosomes that cannot be scanned have a closer look at the structure of the markers there
e.g.: if chromosome 4 was the one that couldn't be scanned:

plot.rf(cross_newmap,1)

(2) Sometimes: Scanning using model="dominance" while there are markers that don't have individuals that are AA or BB
(or in some weird edge cases if an entire chromosome shows no heterogeneity ) the easiest solution is to use the "additive" model
the dominance model is just a subset of the additive model (and thus increases LOD scores in the case of a real dominance effect)

(3) Rarely: Too many cofactors are selected in the initial model. or there are too many cofactors at a single position (this
is related to the window.size parameter, multiple cofactors inside a single 'window' can cause a singular matrix during matrix single value decomposition)

Hope this helps, otherwise you can always contact me directly
Kind regards,

Danny Arends

messages.subject_clean: Toward a more efficient analysis of QTL x covariate interactions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I am currently trying to conduct an eQTL analysis in Arabidopsis and
want to evaluate cytoplasm x eQTL interactions.  Following the
examples in section 7.2 of the rQTL book on QTL x covariate
interactions I wrote the following loop:

k<-1

while(k<=25000){
out.a=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
method=c("hk"))
out.u=scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"))
set.seed(54955149)
operm.a <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, model=c("normal"),
method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
set.seed(54955149)
operm.u <- scanone(dataIM, pheno.col=k, addcov=x, intcovar=cyto,
model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=32)
out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))
a<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, pvalues=TRUE)
all<-cbind(all, a)
write.table(all, file = "eQTL_Cyto_normal_perm_25000_dry.txt",
quote=FALSE, row.name <http://row.name>=FALSE)
k<-k+1}

Unfortunately, even with the 32 processors this analysis runs very
slowly.  I was only able to complete about 350 phenotypes in 24
hours.  I usually can complete about 5000 phenotypes in 24 hours with
one processor using the pheno.col=1:5000 option.  Since my analysis
involves so many phenotypes (~75000), I am trying to figure out a way
that I can make the analysis more efficient, without creating many
scripts.  Do you have any suggestions?  In the end, I need to estimate
p-values in order to implement a False Discovery Rate.

Thank you very much,

David

model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)
set.seed(54955149)

model=c("normal"), method=c("hk"), n.perm=1000, n.cluster=6)

out.u <- c(out.u, out.u-out.a, labels=c("f","i"))
operm.u <- cbind(operm.u, operm.u - operm.a, labels=c("f","i"))

tabbycol_25662<-summary(out.u, perms=operm.u, format="tabByCol",
pvalues=TRUE, ci.function="lodint")

write.table(tabbycol_25662, file = "Tab_by_dry_SNP_cyto_25662.txt",
quote=FALSE, row.name <http://row.name>=FALSE)

Thanks again,

David
